claims.text: As-cast FeNiCrMn undergoes a transition from predominantly dislocation-mediated plasticity toward increasing TRIP activity as strain rate increases or temperature decreases.
The transition to TRIP preserves the strength–ductility balance of FeNiCrMn.
The material is an as-cast, chemically homogeneous FeNiCrMn alloy without additional thermomechanical processing.
FeNiCrMn should be tested in tension or compression over quasi-static through high strain rates and cryogenic through elevated temperatures.
The proposed strain-rate range is approximately 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1.
Deformation produces TRIP-related phases at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Deformation-induced phase transformations evolve concurrently with dislocation activity.
Increasing strain rate reduces the energy barrier for deformation-induced phase transformation.
Lowering temperature reduces the energy barrier for deformation-induced phase transformation.
TRIP activation enhances strain-rate sensitivity without degrading overall strength–ductility performance.
At high strain rate or low temperature, FeNiCrMn will show increased strain-rate sensitivity.
At high strain rate or low temperature, newly formed martensitic phases will be observable.
At room temperature and moderate strain rate, FeNiCrMn retains balanced strength and ductility without pronounced TRIP activity.
Conventional dislocation-mediated plasticity dominates the room-temperature, moderate-strain-rate baseline.
Additional processing or large-scale defects may change the proposed behavior.
In-situ X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy can test whether changes in strain rate or temperature correlate with phase transformation.
Absence of the expected transformation phases together with unchanged strain-rate sensitivity would falsify the hypothesis.
